title: Exception Types
description: Explore the C# exception hierarchy, understand built-in exception types and when they are thrown, and learn how to create custom exceptions for application-specific errors.

data.text: Not all exceptions are created equal. Some indicate programming bugs (like a null reference), while others represent external conditions (like a network failure). Understanding the **exception hierarchy** helps you catch the right exceptions at the right level and write more precise error-handling code.
The Exception Class Hierarchy

All exceptions in .NET inherit from the base `System.Exception` class. This class provides the essential properties every exception carries: `Message` (a description of the error), `StackTrace` (where in the code it happened), and `InnerException` (the exception that caused this one, if any).

data.text: SystemException vs ApplicationException

`SystemException` is the base for exceptions thrown by the CLR itself — things like out-of-memory errors, stack overflows, and null reference bugs. `ApplicationException` was originally intended as the base for user-defined exceptions, but Microsoft later advised against using it. Most custom exceptions simply inherit from `Exception` directly.

data.title: Do Not Catch SystemException
data.text: Catching `SystemException` is almost always a mistake. It includes fatal errors like `OutOfMemoryException` and `StackOverflowException` that your code cannot realistically recover from. Always catch specific exception types instead.
Common Built-in Exception Types
C# and .NET provide hundreds of exception types. You will encounter these most frequently. Each has a specific purpose, and catching the right one makes your error handling precise and meaningful.

rows: Accessing member on a null object reference
Accessing an array/list index that does not exist
Argument passed is null when it must not be
Argument value is outside the allowed range
String cannot be parsed to the target type
Method called when object is in wrong state
Specified directory path does not exist
Operation did not complete in time

data.text: NullReferenceException in Detail

The most common exception in C#. It occurs when you try to access a member (field, property, method) on an object reference that is `null`. Think of a reference variable as a remote control: if it's not paired with a TV, pressing 'power' does nothing — and in C#, it throws `NullReferenceException`.

data.content: Common causes of NullReferenceException and how to prevent them with null checks and nullable reference types.

data.text: FormatException in Detail

`FormatException` is thrown when you attempt to convert a string to a numeric type (int, double, decimal, etc.) and the string does not match the expected numeric format. The best defense is to use `int.TryParse()` or `double.TryParse()` instead of `int.Parse()`.

data.title: FormatException vs TryParse
data.content: Using TryParse to safely convert strings to numbers without exceptions.

data.text: ArgumentException and Variants

`ArgumentException` is the base class for argument validation errors. It is typically thrown when a method receives an argument that does not satisfy its requirements. The two most common variants are `ArgumentNullException` (value is null) and `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` (value is outside valid bounds).

data.title: Argument Validation with Guard Clauses
data.content: Using ArgumentException to validate method arguments — a core defensive programming technique.

data.text: IOException and FileNotFoundException

`IOException` is the base class for most file and stream errors. Its most common subclass, `FileNotFoundException`, is thrown when you try to open a file that does not exist. Other I/O exceptions include `DirectoryNotFoundException`, `UnauthorizedAccessException`, and `PathTooLongException`.

data.text: Creating Custom Exceptions

When built-in exceptions don't adequately describe your application's error conditions, you can create **custom exceptions**. A well-named custom exception tells the caller exactly what went wrong, and allows them to catch it specifically without interfering with other error types.

data.title: Steps to Create a Custom Exception
items: Create a class that inherits from `Exception` (or `ApplicationException`)
Provide constructors that call the base class constructors
Include `[Serializable]` attribute if the exception needs to cross AppDomain boundaries
Give the class a meaningful name ending with 'Exception'
Add any custom properties that provide extra context

data.title: Creating and Using a Custom Exception
data.content: A complete example of defining a custom exception for a game scoring system.

data.text: Inspecting Exception Properties
Every exception object carries useful properties. When logging or displaying errors to users, you should use these properties to provide meaningful context.

rows: Shows the call stack at the point of the exception
Name of the application or object that caused the error
The method that threw the exception
The exception that caused this one (may be null)
Link to help documentation for this error
Numeric error code used by COM interop
Collection of key-value pairs with extra user-defined data

data.title: Reading Exception Properties for Debugging
data.content: Logging rich exception information to help diagnose production issues.

data.text: When to Create Your Own Exceptions

data.title: Reasons to Create Custom Exceptions
items: Your library or API exposes errors that callers should be able to catch specifically
Built-in exceptions don't adequately describe the problem domain
You need to attach extra context (like an error code or ID) to the error
You want to follow the principle of catching specific types in calling code
The error represents a business rule violation, not a code bug

data.title: Overusing Custom Exceptions
data.text: Don't create a new custom exception for every possible error. If callers only ever catch it as a generic Exception, a custom type adds no value. Create one only when callers need to handle it differently from other errors.

terms.definition: The inheritance tree of exception classes, where System.Exception is the root and all other exceptions derive from it.

A user-defined exception class that inherits from Exception, used for application-specific error conditions.
An exception stored inside another exception, indicating the original cause of a wrapped error.
An attribute marking a class as capable of being serialized (converted to bytes), required for exceptions that cross AppDomain boundaries.
An early validation check at the start of a method that throws an exception if arguments are invalid.

items.question: Should I catch Exception or specific exception types?
items.answer: Always catch the most specific exception type you can handle. Use a generic `catch (Exception ex)` only as a last-resort safety net at the top of your stack — never as your primary error-handling strategy.

items.question: What is the difference between Exception and SystemException?
items.answer: SystemException is a subclass of Exception intended for runtime errors. In practice, you should treat them the same: catch specific types, not the base SystemException class.

items.question: Why does InnerException exist?
items.answer: InnerException preserves the original error when you wrap one exception inside another. This is useful when a lower-level operation fails and you want to add context while still being able to see the root cause.

items.question: How do I know which exception type to use?
items.answer: Read the documentation for the method you are calling. .NET API documentation always lists the exceptions a method can throw. Use that information to decide which catch blocks to write.

items.question: When should I create a custom exception?
items.answer: Create a custom exception when you want callers to catch a specific error type that is meaningful in your domain. Don't create one just for the sake of it — if callers would catch it the same way as a generic Exception, it adds no value.

data.title: Lesson Summary
points: All exceptions inherit from System.Exception, which provides Message, StackTrace, InnerException, and more
Common exceptions include NullReferenceException, FormatException, ArgumentException, InvalidOperationException, and IOException
Catch specific exception types — avoid catching SystemException or Exception blindly
InnerException preserves the original cause when one exception wraps another
Custom exceptions inherit from Exception and let you attach domain-specific context
Guard clauses validate arguments at the start of a method and throw immediately on invalid input
The exception hierarchy table helps you pick the right exception type for your situation
data.takeaway: Knowing the right exception type for each situation lets you write precise, maintainable error-handling code that is easy to debug.
